Same given name, same age, same place — but the patronymic is different. Are these the same person? Analyse the identity conflict and either resolve it or say what would decide it.

Note that the conclusion is "these are different persons," which means there is no assertion to prefer — `preferred_assertion_id` must remain null and `status` stays `unresolved` per the identity-conflict protocol. ---

The 1875 census lists a boy named Anders Pedersen, age 7, in Ringsaker, Hedmark — the same given name, same age, and same parish as the research subject Anders Hansen. The decisive finding is the patronymic: in Norway in 1875, surnames were patronymic and not yet fixed by law (that came in 1923). "Pedersen" means son of Peder; "Hansen" means son of Hans. These are statements about two different fathers, not two spellings of the same name. An official enumerator recording a household in person is a reliable informant for the patronymic, and there is no evidence of a recording error. The coincidence of given name, age, and parish is easily explained by the popularity of "Anders" as a first name and the size of Ringsaker parish — finding two boys of that name and age there is entirely expected.

The conflict is recorded as c_001, status unresolved, because the analysis concludes the record belongs to a different person, and the schema does not permit naming a preferred assertion when the conclusion is exclusion. The record should not be linked to Anders Hansen.

To positively confirm what this conflict implies, you would want: a record naming Anders Hansen's father as Hans (a baptism register entry from Ringsaker or a neighboring parish, or another census year listing Hans and his son Anders together), and a separate record naming the father of the Anders Pedersen entry as Peder. Either one, standing alone, would close the question. Would you like me to create a research question targeting those baptism records, or build a candidate timeline for Anders Hansen to test what other records cohere around him?

Both a_001 (the name assertion) and a_002 (the birth/age assertion) were extracted from the same record image by the same enumerator visit to the same household. They are not independent of each other — they are two facets of a single record. The question of whether this record belongs to the research subject is therefore a single-source identity question. No independent record currently links an 'Anders Pedersen' in Ringsaker to the research subject Anders Hansen, and no independent record currently places an 'Anders Hansen' in this district at this date. Treating the coincidence of given name, age, and parish as independent corroborating strands would be wrong: they all derive from the one 1875 household schedule.
added.weighing_analysis: The decisive factor here is not source quality or informant proximity — both sides draw from the same original census — it is what the patronymic encodes in Norway in 1875. The FamilySearch Norway Naming Customs page confirms that throughout the 19th century (the first Norwegian naming law was not passed until 1923) the Norwegian population used patronymic surnames derived directly from the father's given name: a son of Hans was 'Hansen'; a son of Peder was 'Pedersen'. In 1875, Norway was fully within the patronymic era and Ringsaker, Hedmark shows no documented adoption of fixed hereditary surnames at this date. Patronymic surnames were recorded by census enumerators, who were official recorders acting on direct observation of household members — not distant, secondary, or motivated informants. The informant_bias_notes on a_001 explicitly acknowledge this: 'Pedersen denotes son of Peder.' The subject of this research is Anders Hansen — meaning his father's given name was Hans. The record entry is for Anders Pedersen — meaning that child's father's given name was Peder. These are two different men. Shared given name, shared age, and shared district are insufficient to overcome the direct contradiction in paternal identity that the patronymic supplies. In a 19th-century Norwegian patronymic context, treating the surnames as variant spellings of the same name — as one might treat 'Flynn' and 'Flinn' — would be methodologically wrong: the patronymic is not a spelling variant, it is a different piece of information naming a different father.
added.resolution_rationale: 1. The question at stake is whether an 1875 census entry for Anders Pedersen, age 7, in Ringsaker, Hedmark, belongs to the research subject known as Anders Hansen. If the record is the subject's, it anchors him in that district at that date; if it is a different boy, it is simply a same-name near-miss that should not be linked. 2. The census entry, recorded by an official enumerator in 1875, names the child 'Anders Pedersen' and gives his age as 7 (implying birth around 1868). The research subject is identified across other material as 'Anders Hansen.' Both names share the given name Anders and the approximate birth year. The census is an original record created at or very near the time of the event by an enumerator acting in an official capacity — it is a reliable record for the facts it states. 3. In Norway in 1875, surnames were patronymic: a child was named [father's given name] + -sen or -datter. The FamilySearch Norway Naming Customs page confirms the patronymic system was in use throughout the 19th century; Norway's first name law was 1923. 'Pedersen' encodes that the child's father was named Peder; 'Hansen' encodes that the child's father was named Hans. These are not spelling variants — they are statements about two different men. The enumerator who recorded 'Pedersen' was an official recorder, present in the household; the patronymic is among the facts he was best positioned to record correctly. There is no evidence of enumerator error, and two different father-names cannot be reconciled. The record is therefore not the research subject. 4. The coincidence of given name, birth year, and parish is easily explained: Anders was among the most common Norwegian given names of the period (itself following the traditional pattern of naming sons for grandfathers), and Ringsaker was a substantial parish. Finding two boys named Anders born around 1868 in the same district is fully expected and requires no further explanation. The patronymic mismatch is not a recording error — it is the record correctly naming a different child.
